Disease Outbreak Disrupts Fisheries Industry Operations in Taiwan

A disease outbreak has struck the Fisheries industry in Taiwan, causing significant disruptions to the sector’s workforce and operations. The outbreak, identified as a virulent strain of norovirus, has affected workers at multiple fishing ports and processing sites across the western and southern coasts, industry authorities confirmed on Friday.

Several firms, including the prominent Ming Tai Marine Co. and Ocean Harvest Fisheries, have reported outbreaks among crews and processing plant staff. According to the Taiwan Fisheries Association, more than 430 workers have reported symptoms including severe vomiting and diarrhea over the past week, forcing many to take sick leave. In response, at least five processing plants in Chiayi, Tainan, and Kaohsiung have reduced shifts or temporarily suspended operations.

“The sudden increase in illness has left us short-staffed at a critical time,” said Lin Yu-jen, a spokesperson for Ming Tai Marine Co. “We have had to halt some processing lines and delay outbound shipments of fresh and frozen seafood.” Fishing vessel operators have also reported crew shortages, with some trawlers remaining docked in port as a precaution.

Health authorities have launched an investigation into the outbreak’s source, focusing on communal living quarters and shared facilities at industry sites. “We are working closely with companies to contain the spread, disinfect facilities, and ensure affected workers receive treatment,” said Dr. Hsieh Wen-chuan of the Fisheries Disease Control Taskforce. “We urge all workers to report symptoms and follow hygiene protocols.”

The Taiwan Fisheries Association estimates that harvesting and processing volumes are currently down by 18% compared to usual levels for late June. “This is a challenging time for our members,” said association president Chiang Shun-fa. “We hope swift action will allow the industry to recover quickly, but for now, the situation remains uncertain.”

Authorities and industry leaders continue to monitor developments, advising firms to implement enhanced sanitation measures as the outbreak remains ongoing.
